beats.poi_name: Cathedral of St. John the Divine
beats.script_body: Three odd facts make this a fascinating building. First: the largest cathedral in the world isn't St. Peter's in Rome — which is technically not a cathedral but a basilica — it's St. John the Divine in upper Manhattan. Second: despite the popish name, it isn't Catholic, it's Episcopalian. Third: though construction began in 1892, the building is still not complete, and many estimate it will take another 100 years to finish. The 121,000-square-foot structure blends Romanesque and Gothic elements, thanks to the varying tastes of the architects who worked on it over the past century. Most striking, it's being built without steel, in the classic Gothic manner — to that end, in 1979 a master stonecutter was brought from England to train Harlem youths in the art of traditional stonecutting. Much work remains, but what's in place is quite beautiful, especially the Rose Window in the apse, the largest in North America.

beats.source_passage:
Little-known fact: The largest cathedral in the world is not St. Peter’s in
Rome (which is technically not a cathedral but a basilica), it’s St. John the
Divine in upper Manhattan. Odder fact: Despite the popish name, it isn’t
Catholic, it’s Episcopalian. Oddest fact: Though construction began on the
cathedral in 1892, the building is yet to be completed, and many estimate
that it will take another 100 years for that to happen. All of which makes
this a fascinating building to visit. You’ll see a bit of how the ancient
cathedrals of Europe were erected—the 121,000-square-foot structure, a
blend of Romanesque and Gothic elements (thanks to the varying tastes of
the architects who worked on it over the past century), is being built without
steel, in the classic Gothic manner. (To that end, in 1979 a master
stonecutter was brought from England to train Harlem youths in the art of
traditional stonecutting.) There’s still much work to be done (including a lot
of fundraising!) but what is in place—and there’s a lot—is quite beautiful,
especially the Rose Window in the apse, the largest in North America.

beats.poi_name: Cathedral of St. John the Divine
beats.script_body: Services here tend to be among the most musical and progressive in the city. There's the New Year's Eve service, featuring original work from some of the best composers in town; the Halloween concert; and the Blessing of the Animals, held on the feast day of St. Francis of Assisi, usually early October — a ceremony in which New Yorkers bring their pets, ranging from puppies to pythons to thoroughbred horses, to be blessed.

name: Museum of Arts and Design

_pipeline.geocode_source: known_landmark_address (2 Columbus Circle, per chunk; Nominatim live lookup blocked in sandbox)

beats.script_body: It's not easy to get a New Yorker's attention, but this museum does it consistently — it's one of the few museums in town where you'll see more locals than visitors, drawn in by creative, sometimes wacky, exhibitions on design. One highlighted the pins worn by the late Secretary of State Madeleine Albright; another used visitors' sense of smell to explore how perfumes are created. On the top floor, artists in residence work at their crafts — furniture, textiles, you name it — making the exhibits below feel that much more vital.

name: New-York Historical Society

_pipeline.geocode_source: known_landmark_address (170 Central Park W. at 77th St., per chunk; Nominatim live lookup blocked in sandbox)

beats.script_body: When you're NYC's oldest museum, founded in 1804, your attic gets mighty full. In past years that fourth-floor "attic" felt like a treasure hunt, its open storage units overflowing with telling artifacts — a Tiffany lamp here, a pair of historic pistols there, the plaster model head sculptor Daniel Chester French created for Washington's Lincoln Memorial in another corner. Then in 2017 the curators tidied up, replacing the open storage with three not-so-successful permanent galleries: a runway of too-many Tiffany lamps, a room of themed glass cases on facets of city life like "Childhood," "Fire," and "Collecting," and a center for women's history.

beats.source_passage:
When you’re NYC’s oldest
museum (founded in 1804), your attic gets mighty full. In past years that
fourth-floor “attic” felt like a treasure hunt, its open storage units
overflowing with telling artifacts from the museum’s holdings—a Tiffany
lamp here, a pair of historic pistols there, the plaster model head created by
sculptor Daniel Chester French for Washington’s Lincoln Memorial in
another corner. Alas, the curators decided to tidy up, and in 2017 replaced
the open storage with three not-so-successful permanent galleries. The first
is a runway of sorts for Tiffany lamps, with too many similar ones on
display (they’re pretty, but it is overkill). Next is a large room with themed
glass cases of artifacts that illustrate—but don’t do enough to illuminate—
different facets of New York City life through the ages (“Childhood,” “Fire,”
and “Collecting” are three of these too-loosely-related exhibits). The third is
a center for women’s history, which has created several yawner exhibits
since its opening.

beats.script_body: On the lower floors, permanent displays include paintings from the Hudson Valley School and Audubon drawings, making the museum feel more dedicated to art than to history. The powers-that-be had the wisdom to keep the superb 18-minute film that welcomes visitors — reason alone to come here. So too are some, but not all, of the temporary exhibits, which have ranged far beyond the city: one on how Title IX shaped sports in the U.S., another showing how children's books covered the Civil Rights Movement, and a look at the life of Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg.

name: The Cloisters

_pipeline.address: North end of Fort Tryon Park
_pipeline.geocode_source: known_landmark_address (North end of Fort Tryon Park, per chunk; Nominatim live lookup blocked in sandbox)

beats.script_body: An offshoot of the Metropolitan Museum, the Cloisters is the only museum in the United States devoted wholly to medieval art, and it shows its masterworks in a setting that seems airlifted intact from some remote corner of the Pyrenees, or from a castle-lined town in Bavaria. Opened in 1934, the museum was in fact built in the United States, but 30% of its architectural elements — columns, pedestals, naves, doorframes, exquisite stained-glass windows — were salvaged from medieval European structures. It's a stunning mirage: even the land across the river was bought by patron John D. Rockefeller to thwart development and ensure the Cloisters' views would forever have a medieval face. At its heart are four cloisters, garden areas centered with a fountain and surrounded by covered walkways of the type seen in every monastery and abbey in Europe.

beats.script_body: Pay special attention to the Unicorn Tapestries, one of only two full sets with a unicorn theme in the world — the other is in Paris. These richly detailed tapestries can be read on many levels: many scholars see the unicorn as a symbol of Christ, and the hunt to slay it as evocative of the Passion; others read the work as a metaphor for courtly love, with the hunt as courtship and the final tapestry — the unicorn trapped inside a wedding-ring-like fence — symbolizing marriage. Despite this captivity, the unicorn does look happy. They are an evocative slice of a past when nobles only hunted in packs of six, and unicorns were thought to be real — hence the long narwhal tooth in this room, which medieval people believed came from a unicorn.

beats.source_passage:
Though you can see the entire museum in an hour or so, pay special
attention to the Unicorn Tapestries, one of only two full sets with a unicorn
theme in the world (the other is in Paris). These richly detailed tapestries
can be enjoyed on a number of levels: Many scholars see the unicorn as a
symbol of Christ, and the hunt to slay it as evocative of the Passion. Others
write that the work is a metaphor for courtly love, with the hunt itself
courtship, and the last tapestry of the unicorn trapped inside a wedding
ring–like fence symbolizing marriage (despite this captivity, the unicorn
does look happy). Whatever you decide, they are strikingly beautiful, an
evocative slice of the past when nobles only hunted in packs of six, and
unicorns were thought to be real (hence the long narwhal tooth in this room,
which medieval man thought came from unicorns).

beats.script_body: The other must-see items are kept in the climate-controlled Campin Room — bring a sweater. There you'll find Robert de Campin's breakthrough Merode altarpiece, from around 1425, which placed the Annunciation — the moment an angel tells the Virgin Mary she will bear the child of God — in a secular setting rather than a church. It's also dramatic for its use of Jewish objects, including a prayer shawl and a vase with Hebrew-looking lettering, to establish Mary's background. Nearby is the so-called Cloisters Cross, one of only three known ivory crosses preserved from the 12th century — and the most complex, with over 90 figures and inscriptions painstakingly carved into the walrus-tusk ivory.

name: El Museo del Barrio

_pipeline.geocode_source: known_landmark_address (1230 Fifth Ave. at 104th St., per chunk; Nominatim live lookup blocked in sandbox)

beats.script_body: This showplace for the art of Latin America and the Caribbean owns hundreds of pre-Columbian pieces, plus contemporary and modern paintings and sculptures, and — most significantly — 500 Santos de Palo, mostly from Puerto Rico. These hand-carved wooden saints are very beautiful and well worth a visit to see. The museum also throws fun parties for every Latin and Caribbean holiday and hosts changing exhibits.

name: Morris-Jumel Mansion

_pipeline.geocode_source: known_landmark (oldest house in Manhattan, Washington Heights; Nominatim live lookup blocked in sandbox)

beats.script_body: The oldest house in Manhattan, erected in 1765, this mansion was the site of two marquee historic events. General George Washington requisitioned the house after the disastrous Battle of Brooklyn and made it his campaign HQ for four weeks — much to the chagrin of the Loyalist Morris family, the owners.
